text: Fabric organizes its governance surface into four functional areas: managing the data estate (admin portal, domains, workspaces, capacities, metadata scanning), securing and protecting data (sensitivity labels, DLP, auditing), encouraging discovery and trust (OneLake catalog, endorsement, tags, lineage), and monitoring activity (monitoring hub, capacity metrics, admin monitoring workspace).

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Domains let organizations logically group Fabric content by business area or department, enabling each department to apply its own governance settings where those settings have been delegated from the tenant level. Domains can contain subdomains, and workspace content can be filtered by domain in the OneLake catalog.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Governance settings in Fabric operate in a three-tier hierarchy: tenant-wide defaults set by Fabric admins, domain-level overrides applied by domain admins for delegated settings, and workspace-level controls managed by workspace owners for the most granular scope.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Capacities serve as isolation boundaries for compute resources and chargebacks, and the recommended practice is to split capacities by environment stage (development, test, acceptance, production) to achieve workload isolation and cost attribution.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Metadata scanning exposes a set of admin REST APIs (the scanner APIs) that external cataloging tools can call to retrieve item-level metadata across all Fabric items, including item name, ID, sensitivity label status, and endorsement status.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Sensitivity labels from Microsoft Purview Information Protection can be applied to Fabric items manually or automatically through mechanisms such as default labeling, label inheritance, and programmatic labeling. Labels persist on data even when it is exported via supported export paths.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Purview DLP policies for Fabric automatically scan DLP-supported item types on upload to detect sensitive information, generate audit log entries for every detection, and can surface configurable alert messages to data owners when proprietary content is found.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Data-level security controls (row-level, column-level, and table-level) are available beyond workspace-role-based access, and currently these granular controls are supported specifically for SQL analytics endpoints, warehouses, Direct Lake, and KQL Database items.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Endorsement provides two levels of item trustworthiness signaling: item owners can self-apply Promoted status, while organizations can apply Certified status to items that meet defined quality standards. Endorsed items receive priority placement in certain search results and catalog views.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Governance in Fabric is centralized in the OneLake Catalog and powered by built-in Purview: permissions, sensitivity labels, and auditing are applied automatically and inherited across Fabric items, and these controls remain enforced even when data is shared across tenant boundaries.

sources.title: What is Microsoft Fabric? (Microsoft Fabric overview)

text: Purview Data Map can scan Fabric items to extract item-level metadata and lineage, exposing that metadata via Atlas APIs for external services. A live view lets data consumers browse all Fabric workspaces they have viewer access to directly within Purview; manual scanning for full item-level metadata is available at the enterprise tier.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Microsoft Fabric holds multiple compliance certifications including HIPAA BAA, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018, and ISO/IEC 27701. Some advanced governance capabilities (Purview Information Protection, Purview DLP, and cross-org Purview governance) require licensing beyond the base Fabric license.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Sensitivity labels in Fabric, defined in Microsoft Purview, classify Fabric and Power BI items (reports, semantic models, lakehouses) into levels such as General, Confidential, Highly Confidential, or custom labels, and are exposed through public APIs enabling programmatic access by agents and automated workflows.

sources.title: Use sensitivity labels to improve AI Agents accuracy and organizational alignment
sources.summary: A Fabric Updates Blog post proposing a design pattern where an AI skill or agent reads a Fabric item's existing Purview sensitivity label not just to enforce access control, but as a context signal that changes how the agent responds — for example summarizing rather than detailing Confidential content, or declining to touch Highly Confidential material even for users who technically have access.
takeaways: The core idea is repurposing sensitivity labels an organization already maintains as a second signal beyond access control: guidance for what the agent should do with the data, not just whether it may touch it.
Labels remain available to agents through the same public sensitivity-label APIs already generally available for Fabric, so this is a consumption pattern rather than a new labeling mechanism.

The worked example is a report-analysis skill with three label tiers (General, Confidential, Highly Confidential) each mapped to a different response behavior — full detail, summary-only, or executive-only escalation.
This pattern does not change what a user is permitted to see; it changes how the agent composes an answer from the sources it's already allowed to read.
The recommended starting point is a single focused skill/scenario, validated for whether label-based guidance measurably improves answer relevance before wider rollout.

text: Purview Data Loss Prevention and access-restriction policies apply directly to data agent queries, and can block a query from running or strip sensitive results from an agent's response even when the agent is technically permitted to read the source.

sources.title: Fabric data agent creation - Microsoft Fabric | Microsoft Learn
sources.summary: Microsoft Learn's conceptual reference for the Fabric data agent: a generally-available, configurable conversational Q&A artifact that lets users ask plain-language questions over governed Fabric data and get structured answers back. It walks through the question-to-query pipeline, the governance/precedence model that constrains agent behavior, how it differs from Fabric Copilot, and a list of current limitations.
takeaways: A data agent acts as a read-only conversational router that picks the right data source and tool (NL2SQL, NL2DAX, NL2KQL, or Graph) per question, rather than being a single text-to-SQL engine.
Governance is layered with strict precedence: organizational policy beats workspace/role settings, which beat developer instructions, which beat end-user prompts.
Permissions for Power BI sources are looser than expected: Read access on the semantic model is enough for the agent to query it, Build is not required, though RLS/CLS still apply.
Output is intentionally constrained (5 sources max, 25x25 result cap, no write operations, no unstructured files) which matters when scoping what a data agent can realistically replace.
ALM tooling (Git integration, deployment pipelines, diagnostics) treats agent configuration as a promotable artifact, similar to other Fabric items.

text: The OneLake catalog provides a single searchable surface for all Fabric items a user has access to, supporting domain-based filtering and tag-based filtering to help users reach relevant content without needing prior knowledge of which workspace or system holds the data.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Sensitivity labels defined in Microsoft Purview Information Protection can be applied to Fabric items and Power BI content using the same labeling taxonomy already used across Microsoft 365, either manually, by default, or via a mandatory labeling policy.

sources.title: Use built-in Fabric data protection to get your data AI-ready
sources.summary: A Fabric Updates Blog post from the Power BI team framing what it means for an organization's data estate to be safely exposed to Copilot and agentic AI, then mapping that framing onto the Purview-integrated protection controls already built into Fabric: sensitivity labels, protection policies, DLP, DLP restrict access, and Purview DSPM for Fabric.
takeaways: AI-readiness from a security standpoint is framed as four questions: what sensitive data exists, where it lives, who can access it, and how it's protected/observed.
The same Purview sensitivity labels used across Microsoft 365 extend into Fabric items and Power BI content, with protection following the data on export.
Protection policies and DLP restrict-access are the enforcement mechanisms that actually narrow who an agent's queries can reach, since agents operate under the querying user's own permissions.
DSPM for Fabric adds a posture-management layer that surfaces overshared or unlabeled assets and AI-usage risk signals, rather than just static classification.
The article stitches these together as a five-step adoption sequence rather than presenting them as independent, unrelated features.

text: A sensitivity label's protection travels with the underlying data: when labeled Fabric or Power BI content is exported to Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, or .pbix, encryption is enforced so only authorized users can open the exported file.

sources.title: Multi-cloud data architecture patterns using Fabric Data Factory
sources.summary: A Fabric Updates Blog post positioning Fabric Data Factory as the orchestration hub for organizations running data across Snowflake, Databricks, Google BigQuery, and Salesforce. It walks through the native connectors available for each platform, the orchestration primitives that let a single pipeline span multiple clouds, and how OneLake features (shortcuts, mirroring, Purview lineage, Fabric IQ) extend those cross-cloud pipelines into governed AI scenarios.
takeaways: Fabric Data Factory ships native connectors/activities for Snowflake, Databricks, Google BigQuery, and Salesforce, so cross-cloud orchestration doesn't require custom connector code.
A single pipeline can legitimately span three+ clouds: extract from BigQuery, transform in a Databricks notebook, land in Snowflake, all under one Fabric scheduler.
OneLake shortcuts enable zero-copy analysis of data sitting in Snowflake, S3, or Google Cloud Storage, avoiding duplicate storage and movement cost.
Mirroring and Copy jobs are positioned as the two distinct data-movement mechanisms for near-real-time replication versus distributed batch/incremental movement across clouds.
Purview integration is presented as the mechanism that keeps lineage traceable from a foreign source (e.g., Snowflake) through to the AI model consuming the data.

sources.title: Microsoft Fabric Data Governance Tutorial
sources.summary: An independent tutorial-site walkthrough of Fabric's governance surface — the OneLake catalog's Explore/Govern/Secure tabs, a medallion-architecture governance-gate pattern, and a routine governance operating cadence — last verified June 2026.
takeaways: Fabric governance functionality is organized into three OneLake catalog tabs: Explore, Govern, and Secure, each with a different purpose and audience.
The standalone Purview Hub in Fabric's navigation was retired at the end of January 2026, with its insights moved into the Govern tab.
A medallion architecture can have governance gates attached to each layer (bronze/silver/gold) rather than governance being a single end-of-pipeline step.
Enabling OneLake data access roles (OneSecurity) on a Direct Lake-backed Lakehouse can force a semantic model to fall back to DirectQuery, per the post.
Govern-tab insights are refreshed daily from admin monitoring data, so it lags real time and should be read as trend data, not a live security console.

text: A practical medallion-architecture governance pattern applies different controls per layer: bronze restricted to engineering workspace roles with sensitivity labels at ingestion, silver adding schema validation and item-level consumer permissions plus OneSecurity row filters, and gold requiring catalog certification, domain-owner endorsement, tested row-level security, and a completed DLP scan before being marked discoverable.

text: Because Fabric integrates with Microsoft Purview, data lineage can be tracked end-to-end from an external source such as Snowflake through to the AI model that ultimately consumes the data.

sources.title: Multi-cloud data architecture patterns using Fabric Data Factory
sources.summary: A Fabric Updates Blog post positioning Fabric Data Factory as the orchestration hub for organizations running data across Snowflake, Databricks, Google BigQuery, and Salesforce. It walks through the native connectors available for each platform, the orchestration primitives that let a single pipeline span multiple clouds, and how OneLake features (shortcuts, mirroring, Purview lineage, Fabric IQ) extend those cross-cloud pipelines into governed AI scenarios.
takeaways: Fabric Data Factory ships native connectors/activities for Snowflake, Databricks, Google BigQuery, and Salesforce, so cross-cloud orchestration doesn't require custom connector code.
A single pipeline can legitimately span three+ clouds: extract from BigQuery, transform in a Databricks notebook, land in Snowflake, all under one Fabric scheduler.
OneLake shortcuts enable zero-copy analysis of data sitting in Snowflake, S3, or Google Cloud Storage, avoiding duplicate storage and movement cost.
Mirroring and Copy jobs are positioned as the two distinct data-movement mechanisms for near-real-time replication versus distributed batch/incremental movement across clouds.
Purview integration is presented as the mechanism that keeps lineage traceable from a foreign source (e.g., Snowflake) through to the AI model consuming the data.

text: Sensitivity labels defined in Microsoft Purview Information Protection can be applied to Fabric items and Power BI content using the same labeling taxonomy already used across Microsoft 365, either manually, by default, or via a mandatory labeling policy.

sources.title: Use built-in Fabric data protection to get your data AI-ready
sources.summary: A Fabric Updates Blog post from the Power BI team framing what it means for an organization's data estate to be safely exposed to Copilot and agentic AI, then mapping that framing onto the Purview-integrated protection controls already built into Fabric: sensitivity labels, protection policies, DLP, DLP restrict access, and Purview DSPM for Fabric.
takeaways: AI-readiness from a security standpoint is framed as four questions: what sensitive data exists, where it lives, who can access it, and how it's protected/observed.
The same Purview sensitivity labels used across Microsoft 365 extend into Fabric items and Power BI content, with protection following the data on export.
Protection policies and DLP restrict-access are the enforcement mechanisms that actually narrow who an agent's queries can reach, since agents operate under the querying user's own permissions.
DSPM for Fabric adds a posture-management layer that surfaces overshared or unlabeled assets and AI-usage risk signals, rather than just static classification.
The article stitches these together as a five-step adoption sequence rather than presenting them as independent, unrelated features.

text: A sensitivity label's protection travels with the underlying data: when labeled Fabric or Power BI content is exported to Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, or .pbix, encryption is enforced so only authorized users can open the exported file.

sources.title: Fabric data agent creation - Microsoft Fabric | Microsoft Learn
sources.summary: Microsoft Learn's conceptual reference for the Fabric data agent: a generally-available, configurable conversational Q&A artifact that lets users ask plain-language questions over governed Fabric data and get structured answers back. It walks through the question-to-query pipeline, the governance/precedence model that constrains agent behavior, how it differs from Fabric Copilot, and a list of current limitations.
takeaways: A data agent acts as a read-only conversational router that picks the right data source and tool (NL2SQL, NL2DAX, NL2KQL, or Graph) per question, rather than being a single text-to-SQL engine.
Governance is layered with strict precedence: organizational policy beats workspace/role settings, which beat developer instructions, which beat end-user prompts.
Permissions for Power BI sources are looser than expected: Read access on the semantic model is enough for the agent to query it, Build is not required, though RLS/CLS still apply.
Output is intentionally constrained (5 sources max, 25x25 result cap, no write operations, no unstructured files) which matters when scoping what a data agent can realistically replace.
ALM tooling (Git integration, deployment pipelines, diagnostics) treats agent configuration as a promotable artifact, similar to other Fabric items.

text: Governance in Fabric is centralized in the OneLake Catalog and powered by built-in Purview: permissions, sensitivity labels, and auditing are applied automatically and inherited across Fabric items, and these controls remain enforced even when data is shared across tenant boundaries.

sources.title: What is Microsoft Fabric? (Microsoft Fabric overview)

text: Fabric organizes its governance surface into four functional areas: managing the data estate (admin portal, domains, workspaces, capacities, metadata scanning), securing and protecting data (sensitivity labels, DLP, auditing), encouraging discovery and trust (OneLake catalog, endorsement, tags, lineage), and monitoring activity (monitoring hub, capacity metrics, admin monitoring workspace).

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Domains let organizations logically group Fabric content by business area or department, enabling each department to apply its own governance settings where those settings have been delegated from the tenant level. Domains can contain subdomains, and workspace content can be filtered by domain in the OneLake catalog.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Governance settings in Fabric operate in a three-tier hierarchy: tenant-wide defaults set by Fabric admins, domain-level overrides applied by domain admins for delegated settings, and workspace-level controls managed by workspace owners for the most granular scope.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Capacities serve as isolation boundaries for compute resources and chargebacks, and the recommended practice is to split capacities by environment stage (development, test, acceptance, production) to achieve workload isolation and cost attribution.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Metadata scanning exposes a set of admin REST APIs (the scanner APIs) that external cataloging tools can call to retrieve item-level metadata across all Fabric items, including item name, ID, sensitivity label status, and endorsement status.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Purview DLP policies for Fabric automatically scan DLP-supported item types on upload to detect sensitive information, generate audit log entries for every detection, and can surface configurable alert messages to data owners when proprietary content is found.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Data-level security controls (row-level, column-level, and table-level) are available beyond workspace-role-based access, and currently these granular controls are supported specifically for SQL analytics endpoints, warehouses, Direct Lake, and KQL Database items.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Endorsement provides two levels of item trustworthiness signaling: item owners can self-apply Promoted status, while organizations can apply Certified status to items that meet defined quality standards. Endorsed items receive priority placement in certain search results and catalog views.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: The OneLake catalog provides a single searchable surface for all Fabric items a user has access to, supporting domain-based filtering and tag-based filtering to help users reach relevant content without needing prior knowledge of which workspace or system holds the data.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Purview Data Map can scan Fabric items to extract item-level metadata and lineage, exposing that metadata via Atlas APIs for external services. A live view lets data consumers browse all Fabric workspaces they have viewer access to directly within Purview; manual scanning for full item-level metadata is available at the enterprise tier.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: Microsoft Fabric holds multiple compliance certifications including HIPAA BAA, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018, and ISO/IEC 27701. Some advanced governance capabilities (Purview Information Protection, Purview DLP, and cross-org Purview governance) require licensing beyond the base Fabric license.

sources.title: Governance and compliance in Microsoft Fabric

text: The OneLake catalog exposes three distinct governance-related tabs: an Explore tab for discovering items filtered by domain/type/sensitivity, a Govern tab surfacing health metrics like missing descriptions and endorsement/label coverage, and a Secure tab for reviewing user and group role assignments across workspaces.

sources.title: Microsoft Fabric Data Governance Tutorial
sources.summary: An independent tutorial-site walkthrough of Fabric's governance surface — the OneLake catalog's Explore/Govern/Secure tabs, a medallion-architecture governance-gate pattern, and a routine governance operating cadence — last verified June 2026.
takeaways: Fabric governance functionality is organized into three OneLake catalog tabs: Explore, Govern, and Secure, each with a different purpose and audience.
The standalone Purview Hub in Fabric's navigation was retired at the end of January 2026, with its insights moved into the Govern tab.
A medallion architecture can have governance gates attached to each layer (bronze/silver/gold) rather than governance being a single end-of-pipeline step.
Enabling OneLake data access roles (OneSecurity) on a Direct Lake-backed Lakehouse can force a semantic model to fall back to DirectQuery, per the post.
Govern-tab insights are refreshed daily from admin monitoring data, so it lags real time and should be read as trend data, not a live security console.

text: A practical medallion-architecture governance pattern applies different controls per layer: bronze restricted to engineering workspace roles with sensitivity labels at ingestion, silver adding schema validation and item-level consumer permissions plus OneSecurity row filters, and gold requiring catalog certification, domain-owner endorsement, tested row-level security, and a completed DLP scan before being marked discoverable.

sources.title: Microsoft Fabric Production Stability for Enterprise Analytics (2025 In-Depth Review)
sources.summary: A review-style piece assessing how ready Fabric is for production enterprise analytics as of mid-2026, covering governance tooling changes, mirroring/eventing capabilities, and operational patterns (CI/CD gates, retry/idempotency, monitoring cadence) that the author says separate stable deployments from fragile ones.
takeaways: The post reports that Microsoft consolidated Fabric governance surfaces into the OneLake Catalog's Govern tab, replacing a separate Purview Hub.
Row/column/table-level OneLake security is described as enforced consistently regardless of which engine (SQL, Spark, Power BI) accesses the data.
Sensitivity labels are said to persist on data even after it is exported out of Fabric, e.g., into an Excel file.
The post recommends exponential-backoff retries plus idempotent write patterns (Delta MERGE over INSERT) as the baseline for reliable pipelines.
Monthly-only monitoring cadence is called out as too infrequent to catch capacity and reliability problems before they become incidents.

text: The post notes that sensitivity labels applied to Fabric data persist when that data is exported out of the platform, for example into an Excel file, rather than being stripped on export.
